470.t: Ted Dunbar as his closest friend
470.s: Baker calls Ted Dunbar his brother and says no one outside his family was closer, from about 1959 until Dunbar's death.
470.ch: His own groups, compositions and friends
470.q: Ted Dunbar: my brother. Ted, probably, is one source – biggest source of inspiration, simply because we locked in from the time I met Ted, which was roughly 1959 or so, to his death. I probably – there was probably no other human being, outside of family, as close to me as Ted Dunbar.

470.t: Muhal Richard Abrams and Lester Bowie
470.s: Baker followed the Art Ensemble of Chicago in Australia and calls Muhal Richard Abrams a close friend and genius.
470.ch: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
470.q: Lester Bowie. We followed them through there, so we got to be pretty good friends. Muhal and I have remained very close friends, because Muhal was one of the founding members of the National Jazz Service Organization and then ultimately became one of the officers in that organization. So we stay in…

470.t: Nathan Davis and the Pittsburgh jazz program
470.s: A letter from Nathan Davis arrived just after Pittsburgh asked Baker for a jazz program head, and the two stayed close, working together at Ravinia and Monaco.
470.ch: His own groups, compositions and friends
470.q: Nathan I met – I had not known Nathan Davis. I knew Nathan because of his recordings and the fact that he was a big person with Carmell Jones and people like that in Europe. He – it turns out later that I found out he was from Kansas City. Just by happenstance, I had done one of the black music…

506.s: Carter praises DeJohnette's drum sound and a recent recording.
506.q: Jack is a … uh … I just recorded with him last month as a matter of fact with a Japanese alto player. Jack gets a great recorded sound on drums. I mean, it's to die for … if that's still current in the lexicon of slang. Jack asked me to do a project with him. If I could have worked it out, I would…

506.s: Carter knows Pate mainly through his scoring.
506.q: Well, my exposure is really kind of limited because he was in Chicago all those years, and my exposure has been listening to his scoring. When I talk with him, I always … I'm always … uh … trying to ask a real slick question without embarrassing him or me about the voicing for a certain chord and…

506.s: Carter praises Kenny Barron's touch and trust, and recalls his place in the first two-bass quartet.
506.q: He's another … he was in my first quartet, two-bass quartet. He was one of the people, if he calls me to do a project with him, I will make me available. He's got a great touch and again, he trusts my judgment. Not just rhythmically but harmonically, he knows that my notes are not the root all the…

755.s: Kirsh describes Chick as a beautiful, generous communicator; Rowe reads Kirsh's 2021 tribute.
755.q: Yeah. But you know Chick’s influence in my life was just huge. I mean he’s a guy who was a beautiful guy, just a beautiful guy. What you hear in his music is him. That’s his — the spirit of Chick is what you’re hearing and that’s how he was as a person. He was just beautiful, beautiful guy. And…

755.s: Kirsh reflects on their friendship and the privilege of delivering Chick's music.
755.q: I suppose. I mean I think musical brotherhood may be a way to look at it, I think brotherhood is probably more apropos. I think we just hooked up through the process of doing these things together. That was the conduit for the hook-up but the result was that there was a bond there just like you…

83.t: Ruffino's good records; Joe Banashak as a friend
83.s: Matassa credits Ruffino for recording good artists and introduces Banashak, whom he counted a friend despite human failings.
83.q: went through several phases of his life uh at the time of his death i would consider him one of my better friends in the business and this was in spite of some you know human failings that he had and again you know i want to say don't we all uh but he did try for a long time to run a straight…

22.s: The interviewer says Raymond Burke praised La Rocca; he says Burke played with him only once or twice.
22.ch: Handy, Bix and disputes over credit
22.q: He didn't work with me. Didn't work with you? No. He played with me once or twice. Yes. I know Larry Burke. You know who Larry Burke is? He's Jules Kazard's nephew. Yes.

510.s: Rowe relays a tribute from Rick Montalbano, whom Alias credits with saving his spirit; they find a shared connection through bassist Charles Frichtell.
510.q: Mmm, yeah, I can’t handle this kind of stuff man. And vice versa. I learned, him being there during that period of time was like he saved my spirit. He saved my spirit, which at one particular time I didn’t think was going to make it. But him being there, he’s one guy that I would go to lengths to…

900.t: Meeting Bill Watrous in Colorado Springs
900.s: He is nervous meeting Watrous but the two get along after being paired on stage.
900.q: They scheduled me and him to do a tune, two tunes together with a rhythm section at this Colorado Springs. And the guy that booked that was famous for that, putting you on the spot you know. Because he did that to me with Carl, with Watrous and — I never played with Rossolino — but anyway he did…

729.t: Working with Dolly Parton: no creative conflicts, a lasting friendship
729.s: Both were established by 1989; Buckingham says they never argued creatively, he put the best people around her, and they remain close friends.
729.q: She certainly had had a lot of success, going back to — well yeah, from the 70s on for her. And then that’s when I started playing sessions. I mean the first session was really 1969 and ’70. But I was a session player from ’73 on. I started producing records in ’77.

807.t: Friendly chat and Greg Caputo, Joe Wilder
807.s: The two enjoy each other, talk of meeting in person and a shared connection to Greg Caputo and Joe Wilder.
807.q: Your demeanor is so wonderful, I could talk to you all day. You have the right —

606.s: Ellis praises Joe Pass as his favorite guitarist and describes the two soloing at once like a dialogue.
606.q: Well God bless him. I loved him and he was my favorite guitarist and still is. And we had a way of playing. We could play, we knew how to back each other up, but then we could both play at the same time you know? You may have heard us do that. I mean both soloing at the same time. And that, I was…

450.s: Mr. B looked out for her because of his friendship with Klook and her Pittsburgh past.
450.q: Mr. B. You see the color of this sweater I’m wearing, like a pale lilac? When I told you about B coming over and putting his head in the door, this was the color that he was wearing. It was so gorgeous. Because he was from Pittsburgh and he knew Klook so well, he was kind of like my caretaker. He…

558.t: Bebo Valdes as person and friend
558.s: He praises Bebo as the best person he has met in music, tells of their brotherly cards and how they met at the Faraon and Tropicana.
558.ch: Tropicana, Bebo Valdes and the batanga
558.q: Maestro, tell me about Bebo Valdés as a personality or character. Camero Well, as a musician, he was a great musician. As a person, a great person. The best I've met in the music scene.

224.s: Metheny knew his records from Boston; DeJohnette had him play on his first record, and Haynes once gave him a drum set.
224.q: I don’t think so. I don’t really know what – Pat knew more about me than we had anticipated. He used to listen to me with my groups in Boston way back. I guess he was in school then. He knew certain records I made with Kenny Burrell, and records with McCoy Tyner. He tells me those were his favorite…

555.t: Writing for Randy Weston after the stroke; friends
555.s: She still writes for Randy, who she thinks pulled her out of the stroke; her real friends are fellow arrangers like Frank.
555.q: I’ve been writing for Randy. I’m still writing for Randy. I wrote for him up until I had the stroke. After I had the stroke and got over a little bit, I’m writing for him again. I think he pulled me out of it – helped anyway. I thank him very much for sticking with me, because nobody else did.

509.s: She likes Sheila Jordan, a good friend whose work is interesting.
509.q: Yes. And she‘s a good friend. She‘s a funny lady. Yeah.

17.ch: Dancers, Newton, Chu Berry and the Cab Calloway band
17.q: Well he would help, I've seen him help a lot of tenor players. I've seen him help musicians. On a lot of things, talk, recommend them on jobs and help 'em. I've seen him sit down and help them with their music. They would come up and ask him different questions from being out on the road, you know,…

68.t: Friendship with Trumbauer, now in aeronautics
68.s: They meet at Kansas City theater dates, and he sends Christmas cards until his death.
68.q: He says, "I'm in aeronautics." He says, "I'm off everyday like 2:30." So we used to go like a couple times a year at least to play downtown at a white theater and whenever we did that theater, he would always come visit me and we'd go out and have dinner together and he spent the whole afternoon…

231.t: Buck as closer than a brother; benefits with Bill Robinson
231.s: They had a private whistle and called each other Mike, and did charity benefits like Bill Robinson, the King of benefits.
231.ch: Germany, Buck's death and ideas about life
231.q: Yeah. Yeah. He was closer than a brother to me. I felt he was closer. We could understand each other. We had a whistle that we crossed to each other, know the whistle, you know. It was good. We would call each other Mike. He never called me Bubbles. I never called him Buck. I called him Mike. Oh,…

147.t: Meeting Sid Catlett in the early 1930s and their friendship
147.s: Crawford says he met Catlett when he first came to New York and they were jovial friends.
147.ch: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
147.q: Yeah. Sid was a friend of most people, drummers and whatnot. Sid -- people wanted to be friends of his, period. Yes, we were good friends. Big Sid Catlett.

29.s: Howard praises Collette, whom he has known since boyhood, and tells how Collette's father introduced himself.
29.ch: Union career, Masons, mentoring and the Clef Club
29.q: Yeah. He never got in trouble. A lot of the guys got in trouble. [make adjustment] I say a lot of fellows got in trouble, but not Buddy. Buddy's been a very, very, very excellent man to know, and I love him dearly, I really do. I certainly do.

8.s: Garland says he was with Ory on and off for 42 years as his right-hand man.
